title: SOLOMON’S 1,000 WOMEN: Why Did God Allow a King to Have 700 Wives and 300 Concubines?
paragraphs: SOLOMON’S 1,000 WOMEN: Why Did God Allow a King to Have 700 Wives and 300 Concubines?

He was the wisest king of his generation. He built the Temple. He spoke thousands of proverbs. Kings crossed borders to hear him. Yet the man who knew so much about God slowly gave his heart to what God had warned him about all along.
There is something almost uncomfortable about Solomon’s story.
Seven hundred wives.
Three hundred concubines.
One thousand women.
And one haunting question:
Why did God allow it?
Maybe you have wondered this yourself.
If Solomon was blessed by God… if God gave him extraordinary wisdom… if Solomon built the magnificent Temple in Jerusalem… if Scripture preserves his words for generations of believers…
then why do we eventually find him surrounded by a thousand women?
Did God approve of this?
Did biblical kings somehow receive an exemption from God’s design for marriage?
And perhaps the harder question underneath all of those questions is this:
Why would God continue dealing with a man who knew better…and still wandered?
That question is much closer to us than we might want to admit.
Because most of us will never have seven hundred wives or three hundred concubines.
But many of us know what it is like to receive a warning from God…
and keep walking toward the thing He warned us about.
That is where Solomon’s story stops being ancient history.
It becomes a mirror.
Long before Solomon was born, God had already spoken about Israel’s future kings.
Deuteronomy 17:17 says of the king:
“Neither shall he multiply wives to himself, that his heart turn not away.”
The Hebrew is striking.
וְלֹא יַרְבֶּה־לּוֹ נָשִׁים וְלֹא יָסוּר לְבָבוֹ
Ve-lo yarbeh-lo nashim, ve-lo yasur levavo.
In context, the warning is essentially:
He must not multiply wives for himself, lest his heart turn aside.
Notice what God warned about.
Not merely scandal.
Not merely sexuality.
Not merely political complications.
The heart.
לְבָבוֹ — levavo — his heart.
God warned Israel’s kings about the destination before Solomon ever began the journey.
And centuries later, Scripture records something chillingly close to the language of that warning.
“King Solomon loved many strange women…”
Then comes the devastating total:
“And he had seven hundred wives, princesses, and three hundred concubines…”
And then 1 Kings 11:3 gives us the sentence that explains the tragedy:
“and his wives turned away his heart.”
There it is.
The warning.
Then the fulfillment.
God had said, in effect, “Do not multiply wives, lest his heart turn away.”
Solomon multiplied wives.
His heart turned away.
So we need to establish something immediately:
The Bible recording Solomon’s behavior does not mean God endorsed Solomon’s behavior.
Scripture often describes human sin with brutal honesty without prescribing it as God’s will.
The Bible tells us Cain murdered Abel.
That does not make murder holy.
It tells us David committed adultery with Bathsheba and arranged Uriah’s death.
That does not mean adultery and murder received divine approval.
It tells us Peter denied Jesus three times.
That does not mean denying Christ became acceptable.
And when Scripture tells us Solomon accumulated seven hundred wives and three hundred concubines, it is not giving believers a model to imitate.
It is showing us what happened when a powerful man ignored a warning God had already given.
God’s patience must never be confused with God’s permission in the moral sense.
And God’s permission in providence must never be confused with His approval.
Sometimes one of the most frightening judgments God can allow is for a human being to keep walking down the road he stubbornly insists on traveling.
Solomon did not begin as the obvious villain of his story.
That is what makes this so unsettling.
He began with extraordinary promise.
When God appeared to Solomon and invited him to ask what he desired, Solomon did not initially ask for wealth, military domination, or long life.
He asked for an understanding heart so he could govern God’s people.
God was pleased with the request.
God gave him wisdom.
God gave him riches and honor.
Solomon built the Temple.
At its dedication, Solomon prayed one of the great prayers recorded in the Old Testament.
He knew theology.
He knew worship.
He knew wisdom.
He knew the commandments.
And apparently, knowing was not enough.
Read that slowly.
Knowing was not enough.
You can know Scripture and still need to obey Scripture.
You can speak beautifully about God while quietly allowing something else to occupy territory in your heart.
You can recognize wisdom and still refuse to live wisely.
You can have yesterday’s testimony and still face today’s temptation.
You can be used by God publicly while neglecting your heart privately.
Solomon’s downfall is frightening precisely because he was not ignorant.
He was wise.
Yet wisdom that is admired but not obeyed cannot save a person from the consequences of rebellion.
And perhaps that is where Solomon reaches across three thousand years and puts his hand on our shoulder.
Because your danger may not look like his.
Maybe your “thousand” is hidden inside your phone.
Maybe it is pornography that you keep promising will be the last time.
Maybe it is a relationship you already know is pulling you away from Christ.
Maybe it is money.
Maybe applause.
Maybe bitterness.
Maybe ambition.
Maybe the secret conversation you would never want your spouse to read.
Maybe the addiction you have learned to disguise.
Maybe you still sing in church while something inside you has been slowly drifting away from the God you sing about.
Nobody wakes up one morning with a completely hardened heart.
Drift usually happens by degrees.
A compromise.
Then an explanation.
Then another compromise.
Then a justification.
Then a habit.
Then eventually you look back and realize you have traveled miles from the place where you first stopped listening.
Solomon’s thousand women were not merely a sexual statistic.
They became part of a spiritual catastrophe.
First Kings specifically emphasizes that many of Solomon’s wives were foreign women from nations concerning which Israel had been warned because of the danger of being turned toward their gods.
This point must be handled carefully.
The biblical issue is not ethnicity.
Ruth was a Moabite, yet she turned toward the God of Israel and became part of the covenant community—and eventually part of the messianic line.
The issue in 1 Kings 11 is idolatry.
Solomon “clave unto these in love,” and as he grew older, his wives turned his heart after other gods.
The man who built a house for the name of the LORD eventually built high places associated with false worship.
Think about that tragedy.
Hands that helped construct the Temple of the LORD…
also constructed places connected with idolatry.
A heart that once prayed toward heaven…
became divided among rival loves.
This is what sin does.
It rarely introduces itself by saying:
“I have come to destroy you.”
It usually whispers:
“You can handle this.”
“You deserve this.”
“This is different.”
“God understands.”
“You can stop whenever you want.”
“It isn't affecting your faith.”
Until one day the thing you thought you possessed begins possessing you.
And Solomon proves something every generation desperately needs to remember:
A gift from God is not a substitute for faithfulness to God.
Intelligence will not protect a disobedient heart.
Success will not protect it.
Ministry will not protect it.
Money will not protect it.
Biblical knowledge will not protect it.
A reputation will not protect it.
You can be surrounded by evidence of God’s blessings and still allow your affections to wander.
But Solomon’s story contains another uncomfortable dimension.
Why did God not simply stop him?
Why allow Solomon to make these decisions at all?

Because throughout Scripture, God deals with human beings as morally responsible creatures. His sovereignty does not turn people into puppets, nor does His patience mean He approves of every decision He permits people to make.
God warned.
Solomon chose.
And consequences followed.
By 1 Kings 11:9, the language becomes heartbreaking:
“And the LORD was angry with Solomon, because his heart was turned from the LORD God of Israel…”
God’s response destroys the idea that Solomon’s marriages and subsequent idolatry carried divine approval.
The Lord confronts him and announces judgment upon his kingdom.
The kingdom will be torn.
Yet even there, astonishingly, judgment is restrained because of God’s covenant dealings connected with David.
Justice and mercy stand beside one another.
Solomon sins.
God does not call evil good.
Consequences come.
Yet God’s covenant purposes are not destroyed by Solomon’s failure.
And now we begin moving toward the greater King.
Because if Solomon’s story ended merely with the warning “do better,” we would still be in terrible trouble.
You and I need more than Solomon’s wisdom.
We need Solomon’s greater Son.
Jesus Himself said:
“behold, a greater than Solomon is here.”
The Greek expression is powerful:
πλεῖον Σολομῶνος ὧδε
pleion Solomōnos hōde
Something greater than Solomon is here.
Jesus is not another Solomon.
He is greater.
Solomon possessed wisdom given by God.
Christ is presented in the New Testament as the One in whom are hidden “all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge.”
Solomon built a temple.
Jesus spoke of His body as the temple that would be raised.
Solomon’s kingdom fractured.
Christ’s kingdom endures.
Solomon’s heart turned.
Jesus remained obedient to the Father even unto death.
Solomon’s compromises helped bring judgment upon his kingdom.
Jesus took judgment upon Himself for sinners.
And suddenly the scandal of Solomon’s failure begins pointing us toward the necessity of grace.
Not cheap grace.
Not grace that calls sin harmless.
Not grace that says repentance does not matter.
Real grace.
Grace purchased at a cross.
Grace where sin is taken so seriously that the Son of God bears its judgment.
Grace where sinners are loved so deeply that forgiveness is offered through Christ.
This is the heartbeat of the Gospel:
God does not save us by pretending our rebellion was acceptable.
He saves sinners through Jesus Christ.
At the cross, righteousness and mercy are not enemies.
Christ bears sin.
Christ sheds His blood.
Christ dies.
Christ rises.
And people whose hearts have wandered can be called home.
That means the deepest question in this story may not actually be:
“How could Solomon have one thousand women?”
The question may be:
What is turning your heart right now?
Because Scripture did not preserve Solomon’s story so we could stare safely at another man’s scandal.
It preserved it as warning.
What have you multiplied in your life that is slowly subtracting God from the center?
What started small?
What have you renamed so you would not have to call it sin?
What warning from Scripture do you already understand intellectually but keep negotiating with privately?
What relationship has become more authoritative than Jesus?
What appetite keeps demanding another sacrifice?
What do you defend immediately because somewhere inside you know God has already touched the nerve?
This is where we stop talking about Solomon.
This is where the room becomes quiet.
Because maybe you know.
You know exactly what it is.
And perhaps nobody else knows.
But Christ does.
And here is what makes the Gospel breathtaking:
He is still calling you.
Not because your sin is insignificant.
Because His grace is greater.
Repentance is not God humiliating you.
Repentance is God calling you out of the burning house.
The New Testament word commonly translated “repent” is connected with μετανοέω — metanoeō: to repent, to change one’s mind, to turn in a transformed direction.
Biblical repentance is not merely feeling terrible about yourself.
Judas felt remorse.
Peter wept bitterly.
But the Gospel calls us beyond emotion toward Christ.
Bring the hidden thing into the light.
Stop defending what Jesus died to free you from.
Confess.
Turn.
Ask for mercy.
Cut off the road that keeps carrying you back toward destruction.
And when you fall, do not run away from the only One who can cleanse you.
Run toward Him.
Maybe this article found you while you are exhausted from pretending.
Maybe people think you are strong.
Maybe your family thinks everything is fine.
Maybe you post Bible verses while fighting something nobody sees.
Maybe you love Jesus genuinely, but there is an area you have repeatedly refused to surrender.
Then hear this without theatrics:
Do not wait until your compromise becomes your captivity.
Solomon had wisdom.
He had wealth.
He had influence.
He had access.
He had almost everything the human heart imagines will finally satisfy it.
Yet Ecclesiastes—traditionally associated with Solomon—opens with the haunting cry:
“Vanity of vanities…all is vanity.”
Everything underneath the sun eventually fails when we ask it to become what only God can be.
Another woman cannot do it.
Another relationship cannot do it.
Another promotion cannot do it.
Another purchase cannot do it.
Another sexual experience cannot do it.
Another million cannot do it.
Another thousand cannot do it.
If one idol cannot satisfy the human heart, multiplying the idol will not heal the hunger.
Only God can occupy God's place.
That is why Jesus is not an accessory to the good life.
Jesus is life.
And perhaps someone reading this needs to stop hiding right now.
Not tomorrow.
Not after you clean yourself up.
Now.
Not as a magical formula.
Not to perform spirituality for strangers.
Let it be an honest confession that says, “I am finished pretending that I do not need grace.”
Someone else reading those words may discover they are not the only believer fighting through the night.
If you need prayer, simply write:
You do not have to tell strangers every detail.
God knows the detail.
But sometimes healing begins when hiding ends.
Someone may be standing at the same prison door you once thought would never open.
Then think of one person.
Not fifty.
One.
The person whose heart has been drifting.
The friend who stopped going to church.
The husband hiding pain behind silence.
The wife quietly carrying spiritual exhaustion.
The son who thinks he has gone too far.
The daughter who believes Christianity is only for people who have never made catastrophic mistakes.
The believer whose compromise is slowly becoming bondage.
Or send this privately if their struggle should remain private.
Supporting Gospel ministry should never be treated as purchasing God’s favor, proving your devotion, or earning spiritual merit; salvation and grace cannot be bought.
There will probably come a night when its question hits differently:
What is turning my heart?
But before you leave, remember the man at the center of this story.
Solomon possessed extraordinary wisdom and still discovered that a human heart can wander.
So guard yours.
Do not confuse God’s patience with approval.
Do not mistake His blessings for permission to ignore His Word.
Do not allow the gifts He gave you to become substitutes for the God who gave them.
And above everything else, do not let shame convince you that because you wandered, you can never come home.
The Bible is filled with deeply flawed people precisely because its ultimate Hero is not Solomon.
Not David.
Not Peter.
Not you.
Not me.
Jesus Christ.
The King whose heart never turned away.
The King who did not exploit His power but humbled Himself.
The King who came looking for sinners.
The King who carried a cross.
The King who was buried.
The King who rose.
The King who still receives repentant people with scarred histories and divided hearts and begins making them new.
Solomon’s thousand women tell us what happens when the heart keeps reaching for what cannot satisfy.
The cross tells us what God was willing to do to bring wandering hearts home.
So repent where repentance is needed.
Receive the mercy Christ offers.
Then get up and follow Him.
Because your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter when your life is surrendered to Jesus.
The scandal may explain where you have been—but grace can change where you are going.
